utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before the Prosecution calls its next witness, which will be Mr. Theunens, who has produced an expert report, there were two issues, I think, pending. The first was that, and this has been expressed in an e-mail and it is now put on the record, the Gotovina Defence, I think, emphasised how important it was to establish the exact scope of the expertise of Mr. Theunens. We have considered that. Of course, we could invite the parties to make submissions on the matter at this moment, but the Chamber gives the following suggestion. That before we start hearing the evidence by Mr. Theunens on the substance of his expert report, that an opportunity will be given to the parties to further explore any relevance, facts in relation to the scope and the nature of the expertise of Mr. Theunens, and to do that, as a separate section of hearing the evidence, which would mean, Mr. Waespi, that you could put relevant questions to the witness in this respect, that then an opportunity would be given to the Defence to put questions in relation to that, not yet going into the substance. And of course this does not preclude any further questions during the examination-in-chief or cross-examination on the matter, but in this way, the information thus elicited from Mr. Theunens may assist the Chamber in the exercise of its function to supervise the presentation of the evidence through this witness. That would be the suggestion by the Chamber. If there would be an urgent need to make further submissions after questions were put to the witness in this respect, the Chamber will then consider whether an opportunity will be given for that, of course on the basis of the reasons invoked by the parties to make any such further submissions. That is one issue. May I -- this is the suggestion by the Chamber, how to proceed. If you would have short comments on that, either you, Mr. Waespi, either you, Mr. Kehoe, then the Chamber would like to hear it now before finally determining how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The extensive part of my examination-in-chief will be methodology and also his, indeed, expertise in this area. And I suggest that I will weave in your comments, your suggestions into that part of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And any comments on making this a separate -- separate portion, a separate section at the beginning of the testimony before we come to the substance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That will be. The first part is -- you might have seen my outline of -- of topics and documents to be discussed and the first section is background, CV, methodology, and I think that's a good --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would more or less cover the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the suggestion, therefore, is that you would be given an opportunity after this first portion of the examination to, and that of course is not only you but also the other Defence counsel, to cross-examine the witness on this specific subject, again, for the Chamber in order to be assisted in the exercise of the supervision of the whole of the testimony of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously the Prosecution has presented Mr. Theunens, as Your Honour reflected in paragraph 25 of your order, as an expert in armed conflict, structure, command and control, discipline, et cetera. Very broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And very general. And of course the Chamber, in view of the concerns expressed, and apparently living with the Defence teams, the Chamber wanted to respond to that in this procedural way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. On that score, as a practical matter, once the -- if we can ask the Chamber to make some decision as to his degree of expertise because then the questioning changes per paragraph 29 of Your Honour's order, in the sense that Your Honour -- the Chamber wrote in paragraph 29, second sentence: "Opinions of Theunens that fall outside his field of expertise will be treated like other pieces of opinion evidence which means that the Chamber would disregard it unless the Prosecution properly explores the basis for it." On that score, Your Honour it would be important during this supposed voir dire process on the witness's background to have some indication from the Chamber as to what fields of expertise the Chamber considers that Mr. Theunens possesses as opposed to items which are merely his opinion, because they fall outside those fields of expertise. And if I may, Judge, that becomes -- if I may just finish. I'm sorry, counsel, if I can just finish. It becomes paramount because of, and I may be reading this improperly and I can stand corrected if I am, in paragraph 26 of the order, it would appear that to the extent documents are put in evidence or in evidence in conjunction with Mr. Theunens's report, the Chamber will view those accordingly. If, however, a document, and there are hundreds and hundreds of documents that are footnoted in Mr. Theunens's report, if, however, a document is not put into evidence and Mr. Theunens opines on that document, it would appear that that -- and I may be reading this improperly. It appears that there is a shifting of the burden to the Defence of challenging that particular item, and absent that, the Court will consider that opinion as opposed to compelling the Prosecution to establish the validity of that opinion. They are two issues that, while in conversation before the chamber, they appear to be discrete but they are very much interconnected and they put the Defence in a bit of a difficult posture because of the melding of the two. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like that add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I see now we're going to the argument of what the scope, again, is of the expert, and I believe, Mr. President, that the Defence is mistaken. The interpretation of the Trial Chamber's order would require the Prosecution to rebuild the entire expert report and addendum during examination-in-chief if that was true, what Mr. Kehoe said, by specifically delineating each individual opinion expressed in the report, and then exploring the basis for the witness's expertise to offer each of these individual opinions. And such an interpretation, Mr. President, is clearly against paragraph 30 of your decision in which the Trial Chamber directs the Prosecution to limit its examination-in-chief to controversial matters of central importance. This enforced limitation necessarily contemplates the existence of opinions on conclusions contained in the expert report which, although relevant, probative and admissible, are not controversial or of central importance to the case. In relation to the field of expertise, as Mr. Kehoe started, Your Honours in your decision, paragraph 25, you accepted that Mr. Theunens has expertise as an expert on Croatian armed forces system and you quoted: "Our proposition that he is an expert of command and control, military discipline, armed conflict, as it existed and was applied in 1995, and we refer to his 16 years of experience, to his reports he has given while a member of OTP." Therefore, Mr. Theunens does not need to be an independent expert on command and control, the law of armed conflict, et cetera, or on the application of international humanitarian law. In relation to paragraph 29, of course, if Mr. Theunens ventures, being asked or independently, on issues such as ballistics or something else very, very specific which clearly falls outside of his expertise, then, Mr. President, that's my interpretation of paragraph 29 of your decision, second sentence, then I have to lay a specific foundation as to his expertise in these areas; but generally, Mr. President, that is my interpretation, you accepted him as an expert on all these issues covered in the expert report. But of course I will endeavour, as said in my part, methodology to explore all the background that entitles him to be an expert and to provide these opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect to my learned friend, the argument that the Prosecutor proposes is that because somebody is a physician, ergo that person is an expert in oncology, radiology and any number of areas of medicine. Mr. Theunens had a distinguished career as an intelligence officer and that's what he is, an intelligence officer. He is not expert in command and control. He is not an expert in combat or armed conflict, as the Prosecution sets forth. What we have attempted to do prior to coming in here today was to get a delineation of the actual opinions by Mr. Theunens that he was going to make from this 700-page report so that we could address those opinions and those opinions alone. That has not happened. We are faced with a document that the Prosecution maintains is an expert opinion on topics in the military sphere from A to Z, topics about which, for instance, Croatian law. Is Mr. Theunens an expert in Croatian law? Theoretically, he has done what anybody in this courtroom could do which is actually read the Croatian law. He is not a lawyer. He doesn't have the training that the Chamber has, yet he comes before the Court to make opinions on that. Frankly, Your Honour, in the scope of his -- his scope of expertise per the Prosecution is so large, that what this simply is, is a post-trial brief being wrapped up in the cloth of an expert and put before the Court. Now I'm not saying that Mr. Theunens doesn't have a field of expertise when it comes to military intelligence. However, to wrap his entire CV around all of these topics, strains credulity because, simply, nobody could reach all those areas of expertise in this fashion. The problem with that, at this juncture, is that because in paragraph 25, it is noted that: "If a document which is not in evidence is incorrectly" -- paragraph 26, I apologise. "If a document which is not in evidence is incorrectly summarized, the Chamber expects the parties to address this during the examination of Mr. Theunens and, if necessary, for the correct understanding of the document, tender it in evidence." So we have a -- the request to set out the specific areas of expertise has not been met by the Prosecutor or the areas of his opinions; better still. And we are now faced with a 700-page report plus documents where, if I read this correctly and I may be reading it incorrectly, Your Honour, if we don't go through the exercise of challenging this with these documents, then the matter comes in unchallenged and unchallenged in a fashion that could be accepted as the opinion of -- of an expert. It puts us in a difficult position, an untenable position I might add, given the scope of this report. And, Judge, I thought that a simple way around this and on these issues was to have the Prosecution tell us the opinions, what are they, 10, 15, whatever they happen to be, and that we could address those concretely. I think that that is what Your Honour was contemplating in paragraphs 30 through 31. That has not been forthcoming. And as a consequence, we are now in this endeavour of challenging this witness on a 700-page report, and all the items in there, even those which -- it's not clear if he is rendering an opinion on or not. It just makes it very difficult at this juncture to operate in the fashion that the Prosecution has put before the Chamber. I have nothing further on that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I earlier said that of course this would be -- opportunities to would be given to other Defence counsel as well. I usually wait until you are on your feet. You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm hiding behind Mr Kehoe at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- but he's sat down. Your Honour, the issue that the Court should have in mind on this expertise is the questions that have been referred by the Prosecution to the witness, which are not apparent in the text of his report. We have been served a schedule of documents by Mr. Waespi in the last few days, and tab 2 of his bundle, for those who have that, produces Exhibit 65 ter 6111, and there are ten headings, the first of which is: Please identify documents that indicate the defence structures that existed in the Republic of Croatia in August 1995. The next topic is: Please identify documents that reflect the system of command and control in the HV, Croatian army, in 1995. Topic 3, I don't know whether it is on Your Honours' screens yet, is: Please identify documents that reflect the rule and regulations relating to the application of the Laws of Armed Conflict, Geneva Conventions, in the Croatian army. 4, is likewise: Specify, identify documents related to command and control structure, including the exercise of command and control, in connection with Operation Storm, and related operations. Such documents should include those which relate to de jure command and de facto command. So, again, Croatian army specific. Please identify, in 5: Documents that reflect the units that were involved in Operation Storm and its aftermath and their activities. Again, Croatian army specific. 6: Please identify documents reflecting the commission of crimes during or in the afternoon -- aftermath of Operation Storm, including reporting of crimes, Croatian army specific, relating to the military structures of the Croatian army. Please identify all documents relating to the planning, execution or purpose of psy-ops activities; again, Croatian army. Please identify all documents relating to the interaction between the civilian and military authorities. My apologies to the booths. Croatian army specific as well as civilian society specific of Croatia. So the government of Croatia's civilian structures. Please identify all documents reflecting orders to ensure application of laws of armed conflict or other protections relating to civilians or other protected persons or property, immediately preceding, during, or in the aftermath of Operation Storm. So Croatian army -- Croatian army specific as well as civilian society of government of Croatia, Republic of Croatia specific. Please identify all documents relating to measures taken to verify the implementation of any orders under item 9. Again, Croatian civil society, military structures specific. Considering the curriculum vitae of Mr. Theunens, there is very little in there, if at all, that shows his qualifications to speak on those subjects. Firstly pointing out the structures of the Croatian military, as in 1995, in relation to Operation Storm in 1995 and related operations. Secondly, in relation to Croatian civilian government. His qualifications in relation to providing expertise on Croatian government and its structures for civilian society. It was the Prosecution's choice to use this person as an expert. They have their own reasons for that. But the areas of expertise that Your Honours are -- are seeking assistance upon relate to those aspects of civilian society, specifically prior to Operation Storm and immediately afterwards, relating to events in Knin as well as elsewhere in the Republic of Croatia. Remember the allegation in this case is one of a joint criminal enterprise. As well as the Croatian armed forces, military structure. Now that sort of expertise comes from someone either working within the Croatian military system and civil government themselves, or who has made a study of such subjects in a way that is recognised as putting them in a position to give an authoritative opinion. Our submission is that, looking at the CV within tab 1, that there is very little within that CV to commend itself to the Court as providing the foundation for the opinions that have been sought in tab 2 and that are reflected in the structure of this report. Your Honour, those are our submissions on -- on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not going to repeat the theme that Mr. Kay had, but for us, it is a similar theme. With respect to the special police, it is being treated as if it was part of the Croatian military, and obviously that is not the case. It is -- I'm not going to get into the specific details now so as not to use the Court's further time, but it is the same kind of issue that Mr. Kay has with respect to his client that we have with respect to our client. So it's a question of expertise on the issue of the special police, which is an entirely different structure, operation, organisation than the Croatian military. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just very briefly. Two points. The first point is that, Your Honours, you have read the expert report and you decided over the challenges by the Gotovina Defence, I think joined by the other Defence teams, that the expert is prima facie an expert on these matters expressed in his report, and that covers armed conflict, that covers command and control, that covers special police. So Your Honours have ruled on that. The second point is in relation to the opinions. I have, as mentioned by Mr. Kay and I mentioned it before myself, distributed topics and these topics make specific references to the executive summary and in some parts of these executive summaries, and I will precede my examination-in-chief with these distinct opinions about the -- the case that Mr. Theunens will express. I can just give one example in relation to Mr. Kay's client, Mr. Cermak, he says, the expert in the executive summary, paragraph 49: "Cermak is the most senior authority in Knin and superior to the MP and civilian police in Knin." That's the opinion, the conclusion this expert provides, and I will ask him, obviously, for the foundations of that. And then he can be challenged. So I believe Mr. President in some, as I said before, that the expertise of Mr. Theunens, as materialised in his report, has been accepted by Your Honours. And if there is, according to paragraph 29: "Issues that fall clearly outside this fairly broad expertise, not just as a military intelligence person by training but by the skills, the expertise, the knowledge he has acquired over time," 16 years, we'll go into that when the witness testifies, plus the OTP experience clearly qualifies to pronounce opinions as he did on all the relevant military matters sought by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. With all due respect to my learned friend and to Mr. Theunens, and I'm sure that is he an excellent intelligence officer, but what he has done is collected documents. That's essentially what he has done. Any number of people in this courtroom, not the least of which is my colleague Mr. Misetic, could do the same thing. We are talking about fields of expertise. And the fact of the matter is that as an intel officer and not a lawyer and not someone who has experience or very minor experience in the armed forces and none in combat, his appearance -- his appearance, his opinions on that score are not very valuable. Now, the problem as posited by my learned friend is this: Well, yes, he has put some discrete topics out in his e-mail to us, and we appreciate that greatly, but in conjunction with that, he also informed us that the Prosecution was going to stand by the rest of this report and put that in as well. So even though it wasn't addressed directly during the OTP's examination, it was nonetheless going to be offered into evidence so that it can be used by the Trial Chamber down the line on any number of opinions, some of which the OTP never even asked the witness to opine on. The issue at this point, Your Honour -- and I do believe in paragraph 29 the Chamber contemplated some limitation on the fields of expertise of this witness. If not, there would be no reason to make this distinction between comments that are made within/without his field of expertise as set forth in paragraph 29. If we look at Mr. Theunens's CV and give him as much credit as possible for everything that is in there, his expertise is limited to the field of military intelligence. Now I'm not saying that there isn't items in there can be discussed quite broadly, but to talk about all other issues in conjunction with that such as opining on what Croatian law or what military law in the Republic of Croatia means and transpires without any training in that, I submit to Your Honour that is a bit beyond the pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a follow-up in reply. Taking the example that Mr. Waespi just did, and this shows the devil of this matter, if I may say so, his paragraph 49 assertion: "Cermak is the most senior authority in Knin and superior to the military police and civilian police in Knin." Well, we've heard a lot of evidence from the witnesses in this case that take issue with that, that contradict it, and that is something that the Court is entitled to take into account. But, when you look through this CV, there is nothing within this witness's very distinguished career that provides him with the authoritative status to express an opinion on the background to that statement. There are many people in the world with a CV such as this, and many of them, I suggest, would -- all of them would suggest -- I would suggest would hesitate from giving opinions on the subjects that he is being asked to do so by the Prosecution. The details of the matters here fall far short of the expertise that is being sought from him by the Prosecution, and the danger is that Your Honours get an expert opinion suiting a party that is flawed in the extent and knowledge of the opinion giver. A lot of people may be ready to give opinions on matters, we all know that. But it's how authoritative that opinion is to be if it is to come into a court of law and be part of the evidence in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Waespi, it's -- it was not my intention to make this an endless exercise. You started, I think, when I invited the parties to comment on the suggestion. Then the Defence, then you. So I think this should conclude, at this moment, the comments the Chamber invited the parties to make. The Chamber will consider your observations, as I said before, when determining how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did have one other issue which we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was another issue, and I don't know whether you had the same on your mind or not, because when talking about expertise, we're talking about delineation of expertise, and you also raised the issue of the reverse of the burden of proof, which was of some concern to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can I add one issue on the motion to compel, the prior draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the other matter I had on my mind, having dealt with the expertise. The Chamber of course has received the motion asking for disclosure of prior versions of the -- of the expert report and the Chamber is grateful for having received yesterday evening, although not very early, the courtesy copy of the response which, I take it, Mr. Waespi, was filed this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need to briefly respond to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean I certainly received their -- I would do it as briefly as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, if you would remain within four to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, with regard to the Prosecution's argument that Rule 66 doesn't apply, there have been any number of disclosures concerning Mr. Theunens that highlight Rule 66 as the reason for the disclosure. And I point Your Honour to a letter from Mr. Russo dated 12 November 2008 that highlights that the disclosure was being made pursuant to Rule 66(B), as well as an e-mail from the case manager of the 14th of November, 2008, which highlights that matter. So the argument that they put forward that the disclosure just comes within Rule 94 bis is simply not applicable. Rule 66 is applicable and it does bear on the Defence. I mean, 66(B) will allow us to examine matters that are material to the Defence. What is it we're asking for? We're not asking for every bit, note or comment that Mr. Theunens did. What we are asking for is a particular draft of a document. Mr. Theunens told us in a meeting in January of this year that he gave a copy of his report to the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 2007. Thereafter, there were other inputs down the line coming to his final report in December. But there is at least one concrete discrete report that Mr. Theunens has given to the Office of the Prosecutor. So let us be clear that the Defence is not interested in all these other notes, but they are interested in that particular report. Now I will say to you as well that between the first report and the second report, Mr. Theunens told us that he not only read the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief but he read the Defence's pre-trial brief prior to the filing of that report. That makes it quite interesting when one would analyse the evolution of those opinions. And under -- not only is it covered by Rule 66, it is potentially covered by Rule 68. Why? Rule 68 has got two parts to it. One of which is exculpatory, but the other part of it is: Does the information affect the credibility of the Prosecution's evidence? If in fact it does, or can affect the credibility of the Prosecution's evidence, this is an disclosure requirement by the Office of the Prosecutor. We are hamstrung at this report to say that it does or it doesn't, because we simply don't have it. Now, we were given copies of the -- Mr. Theunens's prior reports in other cases, pursuant to 66(B). We simply ask for a copy of this report pursuant to that same guideline. If the issue, as Your Honour put forth, is one of methodology and an evolution of an opinion, this is directly applicable to that. And I will note for Your Honour that in your -- the Court's ruling of the 17th of November, paragraph 29, in the last sentence Your Honour notes: "The Chamber considers that great transparency is needed with regard to this process and instructs the Prosecution, during the examination, to explore with Mr. Theunens his methodology in this report." The issue of great transparency is paramount in this. Why? Because the Prosecution, number one, is putting forth a witness who is part of the Office of the Prosecutor. Number two, he has written a prior report which clearly changed prior to the ultimate filing of that report. Number three, the Defence is entitled to explore the bases for those changes. Was it through additional education or was it through influence coming from the members of the Office of the Prosecutor? Did the Office of the Prosecutor have a particular point they wanted to make and thereby have Mr. Theunens include that point in his expert report that theretofore had not been included in it. I submit, Your Honour, that that last aspect of it will be borne out during the course of cross-examination. But the issue generally speaking, Your Honour, is why, in the level of disclosure in this Chamber, is the Prosecution not disclosing that document to the Chamber? Why does the Prosecution not want the Trial Chamber to see that document? The burden is on the Office of the Prosecutor to come before this Chamber and make an argument as to why Rule 66(B) does not apply. They haven't done so. There is nothing in their filing that comes before this Chamber that says that it doesn't apply. The only argument that they come forward of any -- worthy of any discussion is it would be too difficult to take a brief as it goes through different iterations of evolution. Again let us be clear. The Defence is not asking for that. We are asking for the discrete reports that Mr. Theunens gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. And we know, based on a discussion with Mr. Theunens, there was at least one of them that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in mid-March of 2007. If there are others, we would like those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay is still hidden behind Mr. Kehoe. Now he appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No comment from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In relation to the disclosure, yes, we explained, I think, very precisely in our response of last night that Rule 66(B) does not apply. Lex specialis is for expert reports, Rule 94 bis. And 94 bis says that the final report has to be disclosed and not draft ones. Second, this was, as we explained, a work in progress. Yes, a draft was submitted to the Prosecution team at one time. There was no, absolutely no interference from the Prosecution team to the expert about changing anything. I'm not aware of any substantive changes. If there was interference from the Prosecution into the way that the expert drafted his report, advanced it after the draft, we would have disclosed it under Rule 68, that's for sure. That is our obligation. We don't feel, based on what I just said, that we had the obligation to disclose the draft report. The first argument Mr. Kehoe made about recent disclosure by Mr. Russo, that was a totally different matter, had nothing to do with a draft of an expert report. These were normal disclosures, I think, because the Defence wanted -- I think, the taskings. As we have seen produced by Mr. Kay, 65 ter 6111, I believe, was triggered by a Rule 66 (4)(b) [sic] request and other material, but certainly we did not disclose under that title a draft, and we're not required by the rules to disclose a draft, a work in process by the expert. If that was the case, we had to disclose in all other cases every single time an expert producing something, gives it to the trial team, that would need be to disclosed. I have not seen any single case, and I have been here for 14 years, that in this Tribunal, and that's just not determinative but that is an indication, one single case when a draft report had to be produced or was produced for which there was a final later produced. I think there were cases when draft reports have been produced because there was no final report available at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, in that respect, could I ask you one question. Apparently there's disagreement on whether Rule 66 applies or not. Now you said it never happened, that draft report had been presented. Was it ever asked? Because Rule 66(B), of course, and unfortunately I, by mistake, took my French version which is as valid as the English one. It starts with, sur demand, on request. Let me -- yes, the Prosecutor shall on request. So therefore if you say it never happened, my question would be, just on the assumption that Rule 66(B) would apply, then whether ever any request was made, because if there is no request one could not expect disclosure which is specifically provided for to be made at the request of the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We received an e-mail from the Defence. I think a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I mean, you said it never happened in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it other cases requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am not aware. I just know that the result -- I have asked teams and I looked at jurisprudence and I have not come at an instance where a team voluntarily exceeded to a request or was forced by a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but was there ever any request?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't know. I just haven't seen any emerging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that information. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. There is nothing reflected in the jurisprudence in this Court that anybody has ever asked for this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything reflected in the -- which specifically says that Rule 66 applies on drafts of expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It doesn't say that, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the claim of both Prosecution and Defence finds no explicit report -- support in the case law of this Tribunal in relation to draft expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will note that the prior reports of -- in Martic and Seselj cases were in fact disclosed by the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to 66(A) and 66(B). And just with regard to the entire matter, the Defence is entitled to explore at minimum the effect that this witness's reading of the Defence trial briefs altered in some fashion his report that he filed before this Court. And -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if I may interrupt you there. You tell us what Mr. Theunens told you, and Mr. Waespi said what was -- what happened and what did not happen in the Office of the Prosecution, of course, in which the Chamber was inclined, as a matter of fact, and I will put this to you now in a different way. The Chamber was inclined to rule, and up till the moment of this further submissions, the Chamber had not yet found -- but of course we'll consider that also after your submissions maybe this afternoon. The Chamber had not found a sufficient basis to grant the motion, but at the same time, the Chamber wanted to express that it certainly is not blind for the concerns you expressed. And the Chamber, therefore, would have suggested to the parties that the parties would further explore the drafting of the report, how the report developed, whether any version was given to the Office of the Prosecution, whether -- well, all the kind of matters you are raising which of course this Chamber has no -- no evidence apart from that it's the position by the parties. And therefore to give an opportunity to the parties to further explore this from a point of view of facts, did you ever give a report, was that 300 pages, was that 100 page, why did it grow so much, did you change any of the conclusions, have there been conversations, whatever, to further explore that matter. And either to do that during cross-examination, but seeing how important the issue is for the -- for the presentation of the evidence, if it comes to that, as a whole, also to give an option to the Defence to request that this would be done similarly to the issue of the expertise at the beginning and before going into the substance of the evidence, if that -- if the answers to those questions would cause us to reconsider what was at least until one hour ago, our provisional conclusion, of course we will then consider that. That is what the Chamber had in mind before you made your additional submissions and I invite both parties to also comment in the next three to four minutes on this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can certainly explore the fact that Mr. Theunens submitted a first report in March 2007. I can tell him what was part of that, what changed after that. I can explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you do not oppose this suggestion and would you object to doing that before going into the substance of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can explore that and certainly the burden is not on the Defence, it is on the Prosecution to demonstrate that this material pursuant to 66(B) is not material to the preparation of the Defence given that there is no privilege set forth by the Prosecution on this score. The difficulty, and we will pursue the matter as Your Honour has outlined, the difficulty being that absent some check on that testimony, we have no way to determine whether or not the account being rendered by Mr. Theunens is accurate. We simply are stuck with what he is saying, and that's -- while I appreciate -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Theunens comes and testifies after he has given a solemn declaration, Mr. Theunens can be expected, as any other witness in this courtroom, to tell us the truth and if there's any doubt about that it can be tested by cross-examining, that's for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate that and I'm sure that he will do his best in that regard, but oftentimes facts are ones that go to perspective and checking any change in that perspective from one -- from one report to another, merits scrutiny of the report so we can determine what caused that. That is ultimately where we want to go. I'm not questioning Mr. Theunens' credibility coming in here and testifying before this Chamber as an officer of the Court. My question is making a determination or asking questions concerning any degree of an evolution of some opinion or changes in those opinions which absent the actual report is, I think, difficult for the Chamber to even ascertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock. Of course the Chamber has to consider how to proceed under the present circumstances. There is another matter. That is, that several decisions have to be read out and knowing that the testimony of Mr. Theunens will take quite some time and also being aware how difficult it often is to find time not to rush to the limit of 7.00 or quarter to 2.00, the Chamber will deliver a few decisions at this moment. Then we will have a break. During the break, the Chamber will consider the submissions made by the parties, and the Chamber will then determine how we will proceed. At the same time, this gives an opportunity to the parties to already anticipate that, if the Chamber would proceed as it suggested, that apart from listening to my voice you could already start thinking about how to deal with the examination of the witness to follow. I first will give the reasons for the decision to admit P986, P987, and P988 into evidence. The decision to admit these exhibits into evidence is to admit them with redactions. By way of a written submission filed on the 8th of October, 2008, and oral submissions on the 14th of October, 2008, at transcript pages 10.568 to 10.570, the Gotovina Defence objected to the admission of Exhibit P988, a report prepared by International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights, to which I will refer as the IHF, on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, or the OSCE. The objection was based on the report's lack of foundation and use of hearsay. Following that objection, on the 8th of October, 2008, the Markac Defence withdrew its original submission that posed no objection to the admission of Exhibit P988 and objected to the admission of the evidence based on the same grounds that the Gotovina Defence put forward. Further, by way of a written submission filed on the 14th of October, 2008, and oral submissions on the same day, which are found at transcript pages 10.568 and 10.569, the Gotovina Defence objected to the admission of large portions of the two 92 ter statements, Exhibits P986 and P987. The Prosecution had submitted its 92 ter motion dealing with Exhibits P986, P987 and P988 on the 23rd of September, 2008. The Gotovina Defence did not file its response to it until the 8th of October, 2008, and the 14th of October, 2008, which fell beyond the 14-day deadline for filing a response, pursuant to Rule 126 bis. Further, the Markac Defence withdrew its original submission, dated the 4th of October, 2008, and filed its objection to Exhibit P988 on the 8th of October, 2008, which also fall beyond the 14-day period stipulated by Rule 126 bis. Having considered this, on the 14th of October, and I will not further refer to the year. If not specified it is always 2008. The Chamber nonetheless decided to consider the objections on their merits and the Chamber heard arguments from both the Prosecution and Defence. This can be found at transcript pages 10.568 through 10.574, and 10.577. On the 14th of October, the Chamber decided to admit P986, P987, and P988 into evidence. This decision can be found at transcript pages 10.578 and 10.579. The Chamber found that with regards to the two 92 ter statements tendered by the Prosecution, the criteria set out in Rule 92 ter had been met. Based on the Chamber's guidance of the 13th of October, found at transcript page 10.480, regarding the Chamber's primary interest in a witness's own observations, the Gotovina Defence objected to large portions of P986 and P987. It objected to every part of Hayden's statement not based on personal observation and any conclusions that were without foundation. In making these arguments, the Gotovina Defence misapplied the Chamber's guidance. Admission of hearsay evidence, as per Rule 89(C), is well established in the Tribunal's case law, and the Chamber will, as it has done so far with all other hearsay evidence, assess the relevance and probative value of the hearsay evidence, in the context of the evidence presented as a whole. With regard to opinions and conclusions of witnesses, although not necessarily to be redacted from Rule 92 ter statements or disallowed in oral testimony, the parties are reminded to provide a foundation for those and that failure to do so will result in little or possibly no weight to be given to that evidence. The second argument raised by the Defence regarded the evidence that witness William Hayden provided as to the observations of Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes. Hjertnes was on the Prosecution's original witness list dated the 16th of March, 2007, but by a motion dated the 4th of February, 2008, the Prosecution sought to remove Colonel Hjertnes and replace him with another witness. On the 10th of March, despite objections from the Gotovina Defence, the Chamber allowed the Prosecution to remove Colonel Hjertnes from the witness list, which is found at transcript pages 403 and 404. At transcript page 10.569, the Gotovina Defence submitted that by introducing the evidence of Hjertnes through William Hayden, the Prosecution would be allowed to circumvent calling Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes to testify. Under these circumstances, the Chamber did not find it appropriate to include those portions of Exhibits P986 and P987, which referred to Hjertnes's evidence. The two statements were admitted subsequent to the redaction of paragraph 2 in Exhibit P986 and paragraph 7 and part of paragraph 26 in Exhibit P987. Exhibit P988 is a report prepared by the IHF for the OSCE. Under Rule 89(C), the Chamber may admit into evidence any document that it deems to be relevant and have probative value. The exhibit, compiled as a result of a fact-finding mission of the IHF to the Krajina area between the 17th of August, 1995, and the 19th of August, 1995, is relevant as it concerns a period and an area both within the ambit of the indictment. The IHF report documents incidents that the mission were involved with, such as an interview with the accused, Ivan Cermak, and his liaison officer, Karolj Dondo, and the Croatian civilian political commissioner, Petar Pasic. Also detailed is a visit by the mission to the cemetery in Knin, as well as numerous details from UN officials and displaced Serbs on killings, looting, and burning that they alleged to have seen. The Chamber has found no reason to consider the IHF, which is an uninterested party, as anything other than a neutral source. The report references its sources where available, including, United Nations officials and displaced Serbs. Furthermore, it is clear that the mission did meet with the accused, Ivan Cermak, and his liaison officer, Karolj Dondo, and Petar Pasic. For these reasons, the arguments put forward by the Gotovina and Markac Defences that the exhibit lacked foundation and is largely based on hearsay were rejected by the Chamber. The Chamber did, however, find that the redaction of part 5.4.6 of the IHF report relating to the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, as agreed by the Prosecution and the Defence at transcript page 10.602, is acceptable, based on the reasons explained previously, in relation to the Exhibits P986 and P987. The Chamber also ordered the redaction of part 6 of the report, as suggested by the Markac Defence at transcript page 10.604, as it is not relevant to the indictment, because it deals with the events in Sector North. This concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to admit Exhibits P986, P987, and P988 into evidence. I will now read the Chamber's guidance regarding the use of hearsay evidence and various issues related to the use of statements given to the parties during witness proofing and cross-examination. On the 14th of October, 2008, at transcript pages 10.573 through to 10.575, the Gotovina Defence sought guidance from the Chamber regarding three issues. The first related to the cross-examination of a Prosecution witness who introduces hearsay testimony related to another witness who was once on the Prosecution's witness list but has since been removed. The second related to whether, prior to making attestations pursuant to Rule 92 ter, a witness should be given the benefit of seeing all statements made by that witness in the possession of the Prosecution, including statements previously given by the witness to the Defence. The third issue related to whether and to what extent the Defence should be allowed to put questions to a witness in cross-examination without any line or page reference to the witness's 92 ter statement or transcript. In reference to the first issue, the Gotovina Defence argued, at transcript page 10.573, that the Prosecution should not be allowed to circumvent calling a witness by essentially having another witness testify about the evidence that would have been contained in the first witness's testimony had he appeared before the Trial Chamber. Therefore, the Gotovina Defence submitted, on behalf of all three Defence teams, that such testimony should either be excluded or, in order to protect the defendant's rights under Article 21, the Defence should be allowed to challenge such testimony by putting other hearsay testimony to that witness during cross-examination. Rule 89(C) allows the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. Admission of hearsay evidence under Rule 89(C) is well settled within the Tribunal's practice. The Chamber will, as it has done so far, assess the hearsay evidence's relevance and probative value on a case-by-case basis. Needless to say, the admissibility of hearsay applies to both parties, and the Defence is therefore allowed the same latitude to employ hearsay evidence during the cross-examination of a Prosecution witness that supplies hearsay evidence. This said, the Chamber emphasises that its primary interest in hearing a witness's testimony is, of course, to learn the facts as established through the witness's own observation. The Chamber therefore reminds the parties, and in particular the Prosecution, of their duty to carefully select the best evidence to present to the Chamber in the most comprehensible and efficient manner. While hearsay evidence may be admitted because it appears probative and relevant to the case, the weight the Chamber ultimately chooses to attach to it will be evaluated in the context of the evidence presented as a whole. Such evidence may therefore ultimately be given no weight if its significance in the context of all the evidence remains obscure. Alternatively, hearsay evidence may come to be treated as corroborative of better evidence. As for the specific situation when a Prosecution witness introduces hearsay testimony related to another witness who was once on the Prosecution's witness list, but has since been removed, the Chamber has addressed one such instance in its reasons for the decision on admission of P986, P987 and P988, which I have just read. The Chamber will deal with this particular kind of hearsay evidence on a case-by-case basis. Regarding the second issue, the Gotovina Defence suggested, at transcript page 10.575, that prior to making attestations pursuant to Rule 92 ter, a witness should be given the benefit of seeing all statements in the possession of the Prosecution, including statements previously given to the Defence. The Defence submitted that doing so would allow the witness an opportunity to refresh his recollection, as well as alert the witness to the fact that there's nothing wrong with providing statements to the Defence. In this manner, the Defence argued that a witness will be full possession of all the facts, the parties will be able to move through his testimony more expeditiously, and there is a diminished possibility that the witness will unwittingly attest to several contradictory statement. Those arguments can be found at transcript pages 10.178 to 10.190. While the Chamber recognises that it is in the Prosecution's interest that its witnesses be aware of all statements made by them and in possession of the parties, it is in this respect up to the parties to decide how to proof their witnesses. The Chamber therefore refrains from issuing any further guidance on the matter. Regarding the third issue, the Gotovina Defence submitted at transcript page 10.575, that there is some value in allowing the Defence to test a witness's ability to independently provide the Chamber with testimony, aside from that contained within his or her 92 ter statements. Consequently, at transcript page 10.575, the Defence requested leave to put questions to the witness without any line or page reference to the witness's 92 ter statements or the transcript. The Chamber considers that there is normally no need for the Defence to direct a witness to a specific page or line when referring back to a witness's evidence given during the examination-in-chief or in a Rule 92 ter statement. The Chamber emphasises, however, the importance of not mischaracterizing the witness's words and thereby misleading or confusing the witness. When a party's characterization of evidence given is called into question, that party will be expected to provide a specific line or page reference to the previous testimony so that the Chamber can assess the accuracy of the party's characterization. In this manner, we will avoid improper reformulations of a witness's statement. This concludes the Chamber's guidance. I will now deliver the Chamber's decision on the admission of the videos P842, P846, P848, and P854, currently marked for identification. By a written submission filed on the 2nd of September of this year, and again by oral submissions in court at transcript page 8332, the Prosecution sought to tender into evidence the entirety of four videos with witness Soren Liborius. These videos record the witness, accompanied by two members of the Dutch police, and two representatives of the Prosecution, driving through a number of villages in the former Sector South, between the 16th and the 21st of May of 1997. In these videos the witness provides a description of the areas travelled through as well as specific information in relation to events that he witnessed in the area in his capacity as an EUMM monitor during August and September of 1995. Portions of the videos, P842, P846, and P848 were played in court on the 9th of September, 2008. These portions were given separate exhibit numbers and admitted into evidence. No portions of video P854 were played in court. At transcript page 8332, the Prosecution submitted that the videos in their entirety would provide the Chamber with a good view of the area around Knin. The Defence did not object to the admission of the separate portions of the videos into evidence, but added that if the transcripts of the entire videos were to be submitted for the truth of what was said on the videos, then the appropriate 92 ter attestation should be made by the witness. In paragraphs 35 and 36 of the witness's 92 ter statement of the 20th of June, 2008, Exhibit P802, and on transcript pages 8332 and 8333, the witness stated that he was able to review the four videos in June of 2008, as well as the unrevised transcripts of the videos, that he made corrections in the transcripts where necessary, and that the commentary in the videos was based on his independent recollection at the time. Questioned as to if he were to make the same comments on the videos if asked to do so in court, the witness confirmed that he would. On this basis, the Defence, on transcript page 8334, expressed that it had no further objections to the admission of the videos into evidence. The Chamber has viewed the videos and concludes that each of them contains some relevant evidentiary material. This material deals with contemporary events that the witness personally observed or heard about in his capacity as a EUMM monitor in the former Sector South. The events that the witness describes in the videos are often also recorded in his Rule 92 ter statements. Further, P820, a map admitted into evidence through the witness, marks the locations that the witness refers to in the four videos, as well as the location of the check-points the witness saw or knew about in 1995. The Chamber emphasises that it does not deem all the information contained in the videos and their transcripts to be relevant. However, in order to avoid compelling the parties to engage in the exercise of splitting up the separate videos into smaller portions, the Chamber has decided to deal with P842, P846, P848, and P854 in their entirety. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber decides to admit P842, P846, P848, and P854 into evidence, and requests the registrar to change their status in e-court accordingly. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I have one small one to deliver. I will do that before the break. These are the Chamber's reasons to hear the testimony of Milica Djurica via video-conference link. On the 10th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the testimony of Milica Djurica be heard via video-conference link from Belgrade on the 29th of October, 2008. All three Defence teams filed responses indicating that they did not object to the motion being granted. On the 16th of October, the Chamber gave an oral decision granting the motion with reasons to follow. The witness provided evidence in this case via video-conference link on the 29th of October. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Chamber may order that proceedings be conducted by way of a video-conference link if it is consistent with the interests of justice. The test of Rule 81 bis is met if the witness is unable to come to the Tribunal, if the testimony of the witness is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it, and if the accused is not prejudiced in the exercise of his or her rights to confront the witness. In reaching its decision, the Chamber considered the advanced age of Milica Djurica, who is in her 70s, as well as her physical condition. An investigator of the Prosecution who visited Milica Djurica stated that she had told him that while she was willing to testify, her mobility was very limited due to a spinal problem which resulted in her not travelling far from her house. The witness told the investigator that because of this she was concerned about travelling by plane to The Hague but believed that she would be able to undertake the journey to Belgrade in car in order to testify. The Chamber was therefore satisfied that the advanced age and physical condition of Milica Djurica resulted in her being unable to travel to the Tribunal to testify. The witness was expected to testify, inter alia, about scheduled killing incident number 2, the murder of her husband, Savo Djurica. The Chamber was therefore satisfied that her prospective testimony was sufficiently important to make it unfair for the Prosecution to proceed without it. Finally, the Defence did not argue, and the Chamber did not find that the accused would be prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront the witness. Consequently, the Chamber found that it was consistent with the interests of justice to grant the Prosecution's request to hear Milica Djurica's testimony via video-conference link, and the Prosecution' motion was therefore granted. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision on there matter. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It took the Chamber a bit more time to determine how to proceed. The Chamber has reconsidered the provisional conclusions of the basis of the written submissions as far as any duty to disclose the previous versions of the expert report. The Chamber has not concluded that, on the basis of the facts presented to it, that there is an obligation under the Rules to disclose a copy of a previous version of the report to the Defence. However, the Chamber gives an opportunity to both parties to, at the very beginning of the testimony of Mr. Theunens, to explore the genesis of the expert report. The Chamber might even ask a few questions in relation to this as well. And if there would be ever any reason to revisit this matter, the Chamber will do so, if the parties ask for it. So that would be the first portion of the evidence to be given by Mr. Theunens. Then after that, of course, then both party also have 15 minutes to explore the matter with the witness. After that the Chamber would invite the Prosecution to, first, deal with expertise, scope of expertise, methodology first. Then to stop the examination-in-chief so that an opportunity will be given to the Defence to cross-examine the witness specifically on that issue in more general terms. Of course if there's any methodological issue on a detail, then of course it might not be a good thing to introduce that already at the beginning, but so that we have a general overview of what is considered relevant by the Prosecution and by the Defence as far as the scope and the nature of the expertise of this expert is concerned so that we have this well on our mind if we hear the remainder of the evidence of this expert; that is, on the substance of his report, the way in which he analysed documents and in which he has drawn conclusions, has formulated opinions on those matters. That's how we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Mr. President. Obviously the scope of the expertise of Mr. Theunens is very closely related to his work experience, his training, so I will lead him through that if -- because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that education, background, experience, is of course -- may be relevant facts for assessing the level of expertise. But we start with another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other issue being the genesis of this report, so irrespective of whether it was -- whether Mr. Theunens would qualify as an expert, but mainly focussing on how long did you work on it, did you ever discuss it, was there any previous version presented, has it been discussed, and these kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further -- is the ruling of the Chamber clear to everyone? Then, Mr. Waespi, are you ready to call Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If ever reference or -- to the report or to the addendum is made, I would very much appreciate if you would give page numbers rather than paragraph numbers, because I have no hard copy with me and I will try to find the pages which is in other way more easy than paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it is it going to be separated 65 ter numbers, part one and part two. That doesn't cover the summary that's the preliminary 15 or so pages in the report, from my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll find a practical way of resolving that. Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I will first explain to you how we will proceed. You'll first be examined on matters relating to what I call the genesis of the report you have provided. That will not take very long. Then the Defence will have an opportunity to cross-examine you on that matter. Then we'll move on to the next subject, which is your experience, your expertise, your qualifications, and your methodology. That will also be dealt with by being examined first by the Prosecution and then by the Defence, and then finally we'll move on to the content, the substance of the report. Now, before we -- before I give an opportunity to Mr. Waespi to -- to ask you questions about what I call the genesis of this -- of the report you have provided to the Office of the Prosecution, I would like to know from you: Has there been a version at an earlier stage which you have presented to the Office of the Prosecution or to the counsel which appear in this case? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. The initial deadline I was given for my report was March 2007, and at that stage, I sent an unfinalised draft report to Mr. Alan Tieger, who was -- who is the Senior Trial Attorney. I may have also sent that draft to other senior members of the Prosecution team. However, I want to emphasise that I did not get any feedback on that draft version, except that the deadline which was initially imposed was extended and that I could continue with the work on the report and finalise it in the following weeks or over the following weeks and months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this, as you said, not finalised report with any of the members, such as Senior Trial Attornies or other members of the trial team? Did you ever sit together and have any discussion on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I didn't. The only thing I did was, for example, I discovered that there were a number of gaps, for example, regulations I would have expected to exist in the Croatian armed forces which, based on my research in the information available to the Office of the Prosecutor, were not available to the Office of the Prosecutor. I was aware that members of the Prosecution team were still visiting archives in Croatia, and therefore, I sent an e-mail, I believe, to Mr. Tieger but certainly to two of my colleagues in the military analysis team with a kind of, yeah, a shopping list of regulations I would be interested in to obtain in order to finalise or include them in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked to be provided with material you considered to be missing in the collection you had available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you change any conclusions, if conclusions that you provisionally had drawn in the unfinalised report, that you came to different conclusions in your final report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, there were -- Mr. President, there were very few conclusions drawn in the provisional or the unfinalised draft in March because I was conscious of the fact that I did not have had the opportunity to review all the material that was available to me. So most of the conclusions were only included at a later stage and I have no recollection that any of the conclusions I may have drawn at the early stage in March was changed, or, let's say, significantly changed in order that, for example, I would come to opposite views. I don't remember such an occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still have a copy of the March provisional report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I kept copies of all the earlier drafts. I mean, even if they were drafts for my own use and, yeah, they're in my computer, electronic versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes people replace older versions by new ones you, but -- so you did not do that. I do understand that. Yes. Would you have any difficulty in providing the March version to the Defence, which is of course not -- Prosecution knows it, but do you have any problems in providing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I have no problem whatsoever in providing that draft to any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Including the Trial Chamber if you want to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course what is to be presented to the Trial Chamber depends on what the parties decide to bring to our attention. Mr. Theunens, you'll be -- further questions will be put to you by the parties on, again, the genesis of the report. It might be that at the end of your examination on this subject that the Defence shows some interest in reading the earlier version. We'll then come back to that if that wish exists. Mr. Waespi. 15 minutes I said for each party, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, I think you need to put your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now going back to the issue of this draft. Can you tell us what changed from the earlier draft you sent to the team in March 2006 [sic] and the final version that was completed, I believe, in December 2007. What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Just a small correction. The draft was sent in March 2007. The differences are that in the March 2007 version there was still headings or titles without any contents following there because I didn't have time to include that material. I had that material available in one way or another, electronically or in hard copy, but I had not incorporated it in the report. As I explained to the President, I had not drawn many conclusions, for example, there was no executive summary yet, obviously because the report was not finalised. So if you compare the December 2007 version with the March 2007 version, the differences lay or difference lays in the fact that the December 2007 version is much more complete and has information for all the headings I wish to cover, except if there was no information available, then obviously I removed that heading from the report. And if you allow me, basically -- without wanting to jump steps, the first thing I basically did was to prepare a structure, i.e., a table of contents for my report which included those topics I considered relevant for the task I had been given. But I assume that you will come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you add substantive sections in completing the report after March 2007. Are there subject matters you discussed later which you hadn't covered before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, we would have to put the two reports together because I don't know exactly anymore what was missing in the March 2007 report. I do remember that for headings or for topics I didn't -- I still wanted to add information, those topics I highlighted in yellow. I mean, these highlights are still available. And I believe, for example, that I didn't have a detailed breakdown day by day of the events during Operation Storm. That is for the second part of the report. For the first part of the report, I don't think I had detailed information on air/land battle, for example, because I expected that there would be a doctrinal manual available within the Croatian armed forces that would be -- that could I use in order to address that topic. I found references in a later manual, one from October 1995, which is discussed in the report, but not earlier. Even though I knew that the doctrine or that concept was applied at an early stage by the Croatian armed forces, and that's why, for example, I finally downloaded a U.S. field manual from the Internet which addressed the topic. But I think when you compare the 2007 version with the yellow highlights on the one hand with the 2008 version, because the structure is for 95 per cent the same, some topics may have changed order, but there is no significant distinction in a sense of new topics, then it will be more clear to see whether or -- what the differences are. I'm sorry to be so extensive. I don't remember any significant differences except for the fact that the -- sorry, the December 2007 version is much more complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now when you say that you expected that there would be a doctrinal manual available, I think or air/land battle, how did this issue come up of air/land battle? Did somebody tell that you it is going to be an issue or did you come to that conclusion on your own? Can you tell us more.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Without going into too many details, Your Honours, I knew from my occupations in the Belgium armed forces that at the latest in 1994, the Croatian armed forces started to adopt certain aspects of, call it NATO or United States armed forces doctrine, including air/land battle. I remembered a press interview given by the late Croatian minister defence Gojko Susak on that issue, including the cooperation between the Croatian Ministry of Defence and the US MPRI, Military Professional Resources Incorporate Company, sometimes from end of 1994. I also remember I -- when I was serving in UNPROFOR I obtained two brochures, which were kind of public information documents, compiled by the Croatian armed forces on -- on Oluja, Storm 1 and 2, where air/land battle was also being discussed, so therefore I considered that an important aspect to include in my -- or to cover in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you know that your time is limited. The witness gives rather lengthy answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. But I leave it to you, you have to manage the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. President, I'm finished in relation to the draft of March. Obviously there is a lot to cover about the tasking of the entire report, but I understood your guidance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While genesis might include the task given, whether it was ever put on paper, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure, I can go into that if you want right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Within the time-limits I set.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter 6111 could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us that you were tasked by Mr. Tieger. Was there another STA who was involved at that time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Douglas Marks Moore, with whom I -- I had cooperated in the Vukovar 3 trial, was also involved at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the original task you received which is here on the screen?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be tender, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, number. Any objections. No objections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1110 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have the next 65 ter number, 6112, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, shortly thereafter you received the first task. Did you receive a more detailed one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I remember that there were discussions at that stage about how to best determine my task. In a sense, that I received -- I had the initial ten-point tasking then my team leader in the military analysis team, Philip Coo, became involved, and subsequently I received a more detailed 17-point tasking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long overall did you work on completing the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Before I answer the question, I would like to explain or seize the occasion to explain that I used this tasking as a general guidance, because basically the tasking I was given was to put documents in categories. Now in -- for three or for four previous trials, I had actually compiled reports which had the same layout and template as the report that is in front of you at this stage, and I suggested or I proposed to adopt the same methodology, because I consider that much more useful, both for the reader as well as for others who may be interested. And basically from February 2007 onwards until December 2007 onwards, I worked on reports in combination with the -- with my work as a military intelligence analyst for other trials and cases at ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In relation to this second task sheet, was there anything you added to it? That's the first question. The second is: Was there anything you couldn't complete of these taskings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In relation to the second aspect of your question, point 10, which is on the next page, interaction between civilian and military authorities between August and November 1995, based on the material I was able to review, I felt that I had a lack of information on the functioning of the civilian authorities. Of course, I had information on the functioning of the Knin garrison command. However, I did not have information on the functioning of purely civilian authorities in the area of interest. And that's why I have not addressed that topic in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about the civilian authorities which you didn't feel comfortable in addressing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, for example, there may have been -- I am aware that -- in the course of August and later on, civilian authorities, i.e., civilian government, was set up in a number of areas. However, the documents I could review or I managed -- I found during my -- doing the searchs I conducted, were in my view not sufficiently comprehensive in order to express views on that aspect. Also I understood on the civilian authorities the functioning of civilian courts, and there too I didn't feel or I was not convinced that I had sufficient information to address that topic. Now, I mean, in December 2007 when the report was finalised, based on the overall overview I managed to obtain from the military documentation that was available to me, I don't think that the fact that I couldn't address these purely civilian aspects is a problem for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, one or two final questions. You said you did not have enough information about the civilian aspect. Did you feel you had the expertise to go into the civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's a difficult question because obviously from my work at ICTY I did not have that expertise. As you can see in my CV, the professional assignments I had in the Belgian military, in particular those between 1992 and 2001, were actually for a long -- to a large extent focussed on civilian authorities, i.e., political aspects. But I mean to answer your question, no, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
