utterances.text: That's all I have on this aspect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, just a few questions on the preparation of this brief. Your first report was filed in March of 2007. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The report was not filed in March 2007. I sent a draft to Alan Tieger and a number of -- and maybe Marks Moore, for their personal use, but to my knowledge, the first version of my report that was ever filed, i.e., handed over to the Trial Chamber, is the final version of December 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when you gave this report to Mr. Tieger and Mr. Moore in March of 2007, you knew when you gave that to them that trial was scheduled in this matter for the first week of May of 2007. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have no precise recollection of that, Your Honours. My -- the taskings -- the deadline I received, March 2007, was, if I remember well, indeed based on a deadline for disclosure but that's it. And of course I tried -- I understand the mechanism that draft reports or unfinalised reports can be filed, and that's why I spent many weekends and evenings trying to prepare best product as possible before March 2007. But I think will it will be clear to you when you look at the report as such, that it would be impossible to compile such a report in two month's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when you disclosed this report to Mr. Tieger and Mr. Moore in March of 2007, you expected that report to be disclosed to the Defence for a trial that was due to start in May of 2007. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, probably. I mean, if this is an deadline imposed for disclosure, I assume that the next step would be that, indeed, the report gets filed and disclosed, but based -- I mean, if I remember well that this deadline was not upheld for reasons I don't know -- I mean, it's -- I'm not responsible or I don't -- I was not involved with the Prosecution team or I was not briefed on actions undertaken by the Prosecution team in relation to deadlines that may have changed, I mean, external deadlines that may have changed or not. All -- the only reply I received is -- was that okay, the March deadline does not apply. You can continue to work on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you sent the report to him in March of 2007, that was going to be the final report in contemplation of the May 2007 trial because you were given a deadline to give it to the Prosecution because it had to be filed and disclosed to the Defence. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the military analysis team I have colleagues who had compiled reports for other cases, and I remember, for example, my team leader at the time, Philip Coo, he had once been given a very short deadline, I don't remember exactly which case we're talking about, but there he filed an unfinalised draft and it was filed as such. Now, I also want to emphasise that except for the initial tasking I received from Mr. Tieger and the sending of the draft, I had no contact with the team. I didn't receive any phone calls. I didn't receive any or e-mails. I heard -- when I insisted -- when I sent the draft in March 2007, I'm not sure anymore how I was informed that actually, well, forget about the deadline, you can continue. I saw my March 2007 report as an unfinalised draft whereby, okay, we had to -- or we, the team, had to fulfil certain deadlines, and I would be given the opportunity to continue to work on that report, or if the report indeed was disclosed and so on, that I could file an addendum which would include all the other information I had not been able to include in the March 2007 version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us that there were no conclusions that were rendered in this initial report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I think I said that there were very -- if there were any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please quote what the witness actually said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, I'm -- I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it seems not to characterize the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... maybe I'd asked the question generally, Judge, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. When you said that there were no conclusions, let's be precise because the witness is now saying, Well, that's not what I said. If you put to him what he said, it should be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you made very few conclusions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly. But sometimes as you will see, I mean, when you look at the draft, I highlighted in yellow like, okay, this means this, and there may be two words. For me that is not a conclusion even though there would -- a conclusion would follow from these entries, but that was -- well, there's only so much one can do -- I could do in the time that was available to me. I was also working for other cases. And as I tried to explain, my understanding was that I could -- even if that unfinalised draft would be filed, I would still have the opportunity to file addendum. Fortunately for me, the March 2007 deadline was withdrawn and I was given more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We would have to examine this March 2007 report with the final report in order to see what differences are there, wouldn't we?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how many drafts did you do that you presented to the Office of the Prosecutor? Or versions, if you will.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: After March, I sent more drafts, I don't know exactly how many, I mean, I can check the e-mails, maybe five or six to Mr. Tieger. And my aim or my goal was to keep him updated of what I was doing. Mr. Tieger knew very well that I was working on three or four other cases at the time. I had to compile an expert report for another trial. For me it was not clear when actually what the new deadline was. I knew that March 2007 was withdrawn, but I had not received information for the new deadline which I find a bit difficult in a sense. As I was working on several cases, I tried to organise my work, and of course what is more urgent you try to do first; what is less urgent you do later. So that's why I sent him more drafts in order to keep him updated of the progress I made and I don't remember receiving any feedback on these other drafts I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Moore did, in fact, give you feedback on your table of contents and approved that table of contents, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah. But now we're talking about the January 2007 time-period, that is before March 2007. You are talking about something else now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Did any of the versions that you sent them -- is it your testimony to this Chamber that in none of the versions that you sent to Mr. Tieger or any other lawyer in the OTP that you received any feedback whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will try to explain it again in more detail. Initially, I received the taskings, the documents that have been discussed recently. I first received a ten-point tasking and I'm mentioned -- I think -- I mean, let's see how it goes, but I believe it is more appropriate to compile a report in the same format and using the same kind of template I did for the other four trials or cases I compiled reports for. Then my team leader intervened. I received a more detailed tasking with 17 points. I looked at that and I compiled a table of contents which indeed I sent to Mr. Tieger and Mr. Moore for their feedback, because for me the table of contents was a starting point. They approved the table of contents and then I -- which was mainly, I think, a conceptual issue, i.e., they agreed with me using the same kind of approach as I did for the other trials. And then I started to draft a report. First draft sent to the team in March 2007. To the team, I mean Tieger and Moore. Only feedback was the deadline does not apply. Please continue. Later on I sent more drafts and I can -- I mean, I have them available. There is no problem whatsoever in sharing them with anyone who wants to see them. Just to show, well, look, this is where I stand, this the progress --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Theunens. I have limited time --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- so I'm going to cut you off here, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, prior to you filing your final report, you read both the OTP pre-trial brief and you read the Defence brief, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I read the OTP pre-trial brief, probably I did, and indeed I read the Defence pre-trial brief, but as I have made the solemn declaration and I know what such a declaration means, I have made other -- similar declarations in other environments, the -- none of the pre-trial briefs, whether it's OTP or Defence, has had any impact on my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, let me go on -- via Sanction and show you the Defence pre-trial brief, and it is page 16 of 53. Mr. Theunens, this is the discussion in the Defence brief of the air/land battle as you can see in paragraph 41. It's a fact, Mr. Theunens, that based on your reviewing the Defence brief, you made a decision to include in your report a review of air/land battle and begin to start learning about that on your own. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I explained to Mr. Tieger that how it came that air/land battle was included. I wish to explain to Mr. Kehoe that I have been trained in Belgian military. Belgium was and is still a member of NATO. I mean, that means that we apply a similar doctrine, including in the use of artillery and the concept of warfare. I agree that we, in Belgium, don't use the -- the name air/land battle, but what I have learned during my training is exactly the same. I can -- in relation to the question of Mr. Waespi, I still remember the interview with Mr. Susak I saw, and I'm not whether it was Slobodna Dalmacija or another newspaper where I had a faxed copy of the article which was translated into English and which I received when I had my professional -- or was, sorry, when I had the position I had in Belgium prior to joining the ICTY. So it is not, with all due respect, the Defence pre-trial brief that introduced the concept of air/land battle to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, was it your March 2007 brief.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: We would have to look. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We would have to look at all of your drafts to determine when you put it in; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, if you do a word search in the -- I have electronic versions of my report, if you do air/land and maybe with a space between air and land, I think you may find it in the first draft. I'm not sure. I have not checked all these drafts before coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, if we reviewed your drafts and none of your drafts prior to the filing of the Defence brief had any reference to air/land battle, and then you read the Defence brief which did discuss it, the Trial Chamber then can conclude that based on what the Defence wrote, you decided to include the air/land battle section in your report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Trial Chamber can conclude is not for the witness do answer, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, putting aside the Trial Chamber, one can conclude that you decided to put air/land battle in your report based on the Defence brief. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, I can only explain what I did. I cannot draw conclusions for others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the issue clearly is whether attention paid to air/land battle was triggered by reading the Defence pre-trial brief or that it was already on your mind to deal with that in the report when you read the pre-trial brief. That's simply the issue Mr. Kehoe puts to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my recollection, Mr. President, as I have tried to explain, my intention to include air/land battle doctrine or a few short descriptions of that doctrine in my report was not triggered by what I saw in or may have read in the Defence pre-trial brief but was triggered by my expertise and the structure I had foreseen for the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last area. If we could turn to page 37 of 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I direct your attention to paragraph 104 of the Defence pre-trial brief which notes that: "On 4 August 1995, the Croatian government decided that civilian police forces, MUP, would take over responsibility for law and order immediately as towns were liberated in the HV." Now you read that, sir, when you read the Defence brief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Probably. But I don't recall exactly, yeah, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you read it, but in reading that, you made a decision that you were not going to look into -- not -- you were not going to look into the civilian structure within the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: What I -- Your Honours, what I tried to explain with civilian authorities is for me like -- yeah, local bodies of authority in order to have public facilities function, to have, like, local authority, like, there is a mayor, then there is a district head, and so on and so on. I meant those aspects with civilian authorities. As you will see from part two of the report, I address, for example, the interaction between the military police and the civilian police during and after Operation Storm in the section on the role of the military police, during and after Operation Storm in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the issue of civilian authorities in your March 2007 brief?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: We would have to look. The documents, for example, exchanges of letters between -- or documents between Mr. Lausic, the chief of the military police administration, and the assistant or the -- assistant minister of interior Mr. Moric, I'm quite convinced they're included in the March draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, your 15 minutes over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I know I've run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry I took a little longer, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Having dealt with this first issue, Mr. Theunens, we will have a break now. We would like to see you back in approximately 20 minutes for now. And Mr. Usher, I would like to have Mr. Theunens escorted out of the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a leftover matter. 65 ter 6112, I would like it tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P1111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1111 is admitted into evidence. The matter of other versions to be provided, we now know that we have a pending motion and we have an expert who said that he has this material available and he would not have any problem to share it with whomever. I'm looking at the parties whether any follow-up ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, we would have welcomed looking at that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them. Electronically would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Electronically would be fine. Preferably, as opposed to paper, electronically would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then -- the Chamber will -- if it would be paper, it would save half a wood not to produce it, but electronically there's no -- at least that argument does not count. Whether there are any other arguments which would prevent the Chamber from inviting the witness to provide it, we'll consider that over the break. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we maintain our objections. Obviously that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections, but let's -- I said we have two issues. The first one is a pending motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other is that we have a witness who was examined on the existence of these documents and whether he was willing to provide them. Now, although we all know that the witness is employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, I take it that the witness takes an independent position in these kind of matters and that, therefore, I -- if there's -- I do understand that you oppose against granting the motion. Is there any matter you would like to bring to our attention which would deprive this expert from his -- I would say, inherent freedom to share with others what he prepared during his work as an independent expert? Also in view of what he explained about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mm-hm. No, Mr. President, in fact we do have electronic version, obviously, available. We can e-mail it if we decide to go ahead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need five because I understood that you wanted to have all the versions or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not aware -- I was aware of the March 2007. I have seen the March 2007 because I had explained there was a Rule 68 aspect to, which we had to review. I am hearing for the first time that there were previous versions, which is very likely given the way he works. So if you ask me to -- to make it available kind of, you know, between the parties, that is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I presume that this witness has stored every day his work product. Do I have to understand the request by the Defence to be that he presents an electronic version of every version he did send to the members of the trial team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood. We'll have a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the Chamber appreciates that you stated that you were willing to share previous versions of your report with whomever would be interested. Could I invite you to prepare two CD-ROMs with the same content, each of them containing those versions, previous versions of your reports, so not the final one which was filed because we have that, limited to those that you did send to the trial team or members of the trial team for whom you worked, so you don't have to -- what you stored at the end of the day, just if you sent it, and you said maybe five or six, it would be appreciated. And if you would give them to Mr. Registrar, he will then -- if even it would be possible to make four, that might even be preferable so that we have one for each Defence team and one for the Prosecution. May I take it that they are stored in a -- could I say -- a non-graphic not a pdf, because we have, I take it, an ASCII format, Word or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, they are stored in a Word format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they are searchable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, if you'll allow me, can I seek assistance of the OTP to provide me with the CD-ROMs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think even the registrar would provide you with some empty CD-ROMs. To burn them you can do that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you need any technical assistance, ask any technical support. I even can do it so it must be ... must not be very difficult. Then we now move on to the next subject. That is, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can I make a comment just on your order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I accepted an offer which is not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But the same situation would apply if it's going to apply when Defence witnesses, expert witnesses are coming, that if they are willing to give up their drafts, that the Defence is not going claim any privilege as to what they are going to deliver to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether privilege is involved, first of all, whether -- the privilege is usually defined as client privilege for an accused. Whether that would amount to exactly the same as privilege in relation to an expert and the Prosecution is still to be seen. It may depend on what confidential material is provided to the expert which was confidentially obtained by an accused. There might be a difference. I take it that you may raise the issue at a later stage, that the Prosecution would like to see earlier versions of expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I don't want to reopen the issue but we still think that despite his independent position, which I accept, it is it our work product which we have also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- a right to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... make it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You reserve every right to ask the same from the Defence and then you mentioned a few legal terms. I perhaps was not wise enough to wait until a later stage to respond to that, but of course it need a bit of analysis. The problem was not easy. Certainly in the future if we are in a different situation, the problem might be as difficult as it is now and then we will hear from the parties, what their positions will be. But I don't think that we should bother Mr. Theunens at this moment with this, who was so kind to offer the previous versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's address issues about your expertise, your qualifications and let me start with your academic qualifications and work experience. Now you received a master of arts degree in social and military sciences from the Royal Military Academy in Brussels in 1987 [Realtime transcript read in error "1997"]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. At the time it was known as an Licentiaat, but with the European regulation on academic degrees it is equal to a masters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll go into more detail later but can you very briefly list the major topics, the major areas of your study?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I see in the transcript it says 1997. It's December 1987 when I graduated. Studies were about military history, social science, like psychology. There was a course in leadership, political geography, ballistics, military law, and various economics courses including management. That is for the purely academic part. At the same time you also receive military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that in more detail. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you have a tendency to speak rather quickly. Could you please try to keep that under control. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi, and could you take a break and check also with the transcript and perhaps on the other channels whether translation was able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we know by now that you are a member of the military analysis team of the OTP. Since when?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I joined the military analysis team in the OTP on the 29th of June, 2001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does that team do, that MAT, as it is commonly known?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours the MAT looks at what we call the military dimension of certain issues, i.e., we assist members of the Office of the Prosecutor with sometimes very basic military aspects, i.e., explaining how artillery functions, what is the difference between, for example, a direct-firing weapon or an indirect firing weapon. More interestingly, we look at -- we analyse evidence in order to establish or reconstruct command structures both from the de jure point of view, i.e., based on the doctrine and the legislation as well as de facto, i.e., by analysing military evidence that is available to us. We also analyse the political military interaction and we try to assist with re-establishing facts related to particular events or developments that members of the Office of the Prosecutor ask us to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you personally, you participated in all these events or activities you just described?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I don't know whether it is relevant to give an overview of the cases I have worked on or the trials I testified in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask you specifically about that. But you did personally participate in all these activities that you described?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And as I have included in my CV, in a number of cases I also participated in interviews of senior military witnesses. Again, I emphasise I have not conducted these activities in relation to the current trial or this trial here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Theunens. We'll come to that in a moment. Now since you joined the MAT in 2001, have you specialized or focussed on certain areas, and if so, what are these areas?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on my previous experience, I was mainly tasked with cases involving JNA/local Serb forces in the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And have you testified before this Tribunal as an expert witness, and if so, in which cases?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I testified in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. I also testified in the trial of Milan Martic, the trial of what is known as the Vukovar three, i.e., Radic, Sljivancanin, and Mrksic. And in February this year I testified in the trial of Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do all these cases refer to matters that happened in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And -- okay, there's -- for Vojislav Seselj there were also events included that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Specifically the Milan Martic case, can you very briefly outline what the case is about and what you testified about.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tasking I received when I was tasked to compile a report was to establish the role or -- I will rephrase that. To analyse documentation in order to establish the role of Milan Martic in events that occurred in 1991, as well as his role in the shelling of Zagreb in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which territory is encompassed with or connected to the role of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is the Republic of Croatia, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And specifically, which part of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, for 1991, 1992, it was -- it was first an area known as, geographically, the Krajina which then became the so-called SAO Krajina which then became the so-called RSK, and Zagreb is the capital of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the reports. Did you prepare any reports before you testified in these four cases?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. My testimony was always based on reports which had the same -- use the same layout or same kind of template as I applied here in -- for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you currently preparing other reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have been requested to prepare an addendum to my report for the Milan Martic case, to prepare an addendum for the Perisic case, covering the relations between the VJ, so the Yugoslav Army, after May 1992, and the VRS, i.e., the armed forces of the Bosnian Serbs, 1992/1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My last question on this issue: Were your reports in these cases, the ones in which you testified, were admitted as evidence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. They were admitted as evidence, and in the cases where there is a judgement, or even an appeals judgement, there have been quotations or references to my reports or testimony in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go into more detail about your military background and experience. You were in the Military Academy starting from 1983. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long did that Military Academy last?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I attended what is known in Dutch, the Alle Wapens Division, or all arms, and that is -- the studies have a duration of four years and a half, so I graduated there in December 1987. And subsequently because I belonged to the army and had chosen armour, i.e., tanks, as a weapon, I attended six months in training in armour school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that. Let's focus on this Military Academy. Can you tell us what you studied there. What were the topics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Your Honours, and it's is also included in the CV that was attached to my report, the courses included military history, social sciences like psychology, sociology. We had law, both private law as well as international law and laws of armed conflict. There was a course on leadership, on military leadership. And there were also technical courses, or call it technical, there was a course on physics, nuclear physics, chemistry, ballistics, and so on, and also management, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago there is a military part of that education. Can you tell us in more detail what that entailed.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In addition to living under a military regime where one has to wake up at a certain moment and make sure that certain aspects of personal discipline are respected, during school holidays we went for military training, and that was, most of the times, light infantry training, as well as later on there was airborne training, hill climbing driver's licence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's focus on the next part of your CV. Those are the six months of armour school you mentioned a moment ago. What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In armour school you learn your job as a platoon commander of a tank platoon, which consists of four tanks. I was in tanks, Leopard tanks, but at the same time we also had a training in reconnaissance, i.e., the lighter tanks which are used, as I mentioned, for reconnaissance tasks. You also learn about the technical aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: After these six months, I understand you were three years part of Belgian forces in Germany. Can you explain in more detail about that experience.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, during the first two years I held the position of platoon commander of a tank platoon in the 2nd Guards Regiment. The last year I was also second in command of the company, and at occasions when the company commander was away for training or education, I was also the acting company commander. The third year of my assignment with the 2nd Guards Regiment I was S1, which is personnel officer, and at the same time I was also the personal secretary for the battalion or, yeah, we call it the regiment but in fact it is a battalion, the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In these command roles did you take away experiences about command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Even though later on I was exposed to command and control -- to the exercise of command and control at a higher level, i.e., not myself but I worked in staffs or in environments where command and control was exercised at a much higher level, I believe that the enforcement of command and control and in particular the enforcement of discipline is the most -- gets more and more difficult the closer you get to the soldier level. Because in general it is very easy to command officers. It's much more difficult to command soldiers because they have a different background, different education, different values, can have -- can originate from various social levels and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you involved in issues of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. One of the tasks, even at the level of a platoon commander, is enforce discipline among your personnel. As in a tank platoon your three non-commissioned officers and your 12 soldiers including -- most of them were professional soldiers, but there were also four conscripts. And as I mentioned these people come from various environments, have various backgrounds but they're humans, and the lessons one learns during education at Military Academy are very useful in a sense that, first of all, you need to have self-discipline in order to be respected by your personnel; and in addition, you need to enforce discipline at any time in order to ensure that people, after a while, after they got familiar with you, become -- if I can express myself that way, more spontaneous in abiding by the rules, but then still you have to remain vigilant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned your role as a commander and you added that you also served in a battalion. In what staff function did you serve in that battalion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: So the staff function I held was S1, that's the NATO acronym where you go from S1 to S6: 1 is personnel; 2 is intelligence; 3 is operations; 4 is logistics; 5 is what is now called CMC, Civil Military Cooperation. We didn't have that in the battalion. 6 is communications and so on. Personnel means that you are responsible not only for the management but also to a certain extent for the enforcement of regulations and you also assist the battalion commander in the area of discipline, with the preparation of his disciplinary decisions. Because as it is in most armies, a battalion commander will have more authority to enforce discipline than a company commander and a company commander will have more authority than a platoon commander. For most of the sanctions -- for most of the -- I'm sorry, for most of the violations, the platoon commander can only report. Some of them the company commander can decide about disciplinary measures or sentences. For more serious violations is up to the battalion commander or even higher. If, for example, one of our soldiers got involved into situations which he presented -- which could represent a crime, and it happened both inside or outside the battalion, the battalion commander would be informed and it would be up to him to take certain measures. And as an S1, you have to assist the battalion commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Theunens. You talked about your role as a staff officer at the battalion level. Were you also a staff officer at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I briefly mentioned the fact that I was doing an exercise, a command post exercise at a corps level. I was a liaison officer during two weeks between two brigade. My brigade -- I mean the brigade to which my regiment belonged, as well as another brigade, and I spent most of the time in the operation room where I, even before attending the courses, I could learn a lot about how a brigade staff functions, how the commander acts, what a Chief of Staff does, and how the staff officers interact with each other and do their work. When I served in peace support operations in the former Yugoslavia in the UNPROFOR headquarters, which became later known as the UNPF headquarters, well, I worked in a -- in a force headquarters of a force which was commanded by a French four-star general, which is a NATO equivalent a three-star general, with more than 30.000 troops. So that was a staff above the level of a Corps Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Do you have any training knowledge about artillery?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mentioned the ballistics course which gives you a very good theoretical insight in the nature of artillery firing, i.e., the fact that there is something known as dispersion and statistics and so on and so on. More concretely speaking, when I was a platoon commander I attended -- I apologise, a one week forward observer course whereby the commanding officers or platoon commanders in what we call combat arms, infantry armour reconnaissance, they have to able to guide artillery fire onto the target. We're talking here about traditional artillery, not use of missiles whereby you have someone who sees the target and who is in contact with the fire control centre which is in the back. And the fire control centre actually directs the artillery fire, whereby the forward observer can, through his visual observation, inform the fire control centre about the results, and more importantly, can inform the fire control centre about any corrections that have to be made to the fire in order to ensure that the desired targets are engaged. And I'm sorry to be so extensive, but when I attended what we call second cycle, which is the brigade level staff course in the Belgian armed forces, it is a one-year course, and there you learn how to organise artillery fire, as well as the use of other support weapons, at a brigade level, which means the choice of targets, the privatisation of targets, you prepare firing plans in order to make sure that the right targets are engaged with the right ammunition at the right time and so on. That concludes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I note -- I note from your CV that you also were an instructor in a Military Academy for a year. When was that and what was your job?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In July 1991, I was reassigned from the 2nd Guards Regiment to the Military Academy to be first - and I will translate the function literally - assistant promotion commander in the -- for the 146th Polytechnic promotion. So I was the deputy to the promotion commander. He left the position in December and then I took over his position, i.e., I became the promotion commander for the first year Polytechnic. My job consisted of coaching the cadet officers in their academic training as well as organizing and providing military training to the cadet officers. I use the expression "cadet officer" because they were not yet officers. We only become officers after making the solemn declaration in the beginning of the third year of Military Academy. Of course when I say military training, it also includes explaining and enforcing discipline to people and explain why military discipline so important not only on the personal level but also when you work with subordinates throughout your career.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the time you spent as a Belgian military intelligence analyst and that's the time-frame between September 1992 and May 2000. Part of that, as you already mentioned, was a detail to the former Yugoslavia. We'll come to that in a moment. Please explain first what this job was about in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission I would prefer to do that in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against turning into private session on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't understand the reason why but may we go to private session to -- to -- or closed session to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think private session would do, Mr. Theunens. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go to the former Yugoslavia when you were working for the Belgium authorities?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The first time I went in -- I believe it was July or August 1993 for a one-week visit to the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, Sector East headquarters in Erdut, as well as BH command in Kiseljak, and Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina. More importantly from December 1994 until October 1995, I was assigned as a military information officer to the UNPROFOR/UNPF headquarters in Zagreb. You also want me to address the later?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. Let's focus now on -- on this part. What was your role between December 1994 and October 1995 and were where you stationed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, initially I replaced the Belgian colleague whose six-month tour had ended, and then my -- and at that time my task consisted of keeping database with orders of battle. I explained to the deputy head of the office and the head of the office of the military information office that I had worked on the conflict before, and then after a month and a half, a new chief military information officer arrived, a Swedish colonel Svenson. He established what was known as the assessment desk in the office and I was assigned to that desk together with Swedish Major Joakim Robertsson, who had worked for UNPROFOR before and who returned to the military information office, I believe, in January 1995. The task was to -- based on the information we received from the military component, i.e., the battalions, the sector commands, the area commands as well as other information, civil affairs, political affairs, open source, to provide mid- and long-term assessments on the possible developments of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, focussed on Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Robertsson focussed more on Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I remember well, and my focus was more on Croatia. And I was stationed in Zagreb, as I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was part of your job to provide briefings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There were daily briefings -- there was a 8.00 or 8.15 briefing in the joint operation of the UNPROFOR headquarters where Robertsson, two other members of the office or myself would give the G2 -- what we call the G2 assessment of the -- on the -- in relation to the developments of the last 24 hours. There was also a briefing at 11.00 for the Force Commander, where, again, we were a group of four who were in a duty role to provide that briefing. And there were also occasional briefings to more senior -- not more senior but to Mr. Akashi, who was the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, as well as informal briefings for visiting VIPs, members of the military and civilian component of the headquarters and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also draft reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. We would draft an internal report which was called the G2, I think, daily summary which gave, again, written assessments on developments of last 24 hours. We also developed -- produced reports which were kind of more mid-term and long-term analysis, and one of these analysis -- some of them were like on our own initiative, others we were tasked by members of the headquarters. One of these analysis was a course of action document in relation to the situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When part of UNPROFOR in 1995, did you make field trips?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I visited the Bihac area, together with a French logistics convoy, in December -- I think it is end of December 1994 or early January 1995. Later in January 1995, I went on a two-week trip together with the incoming head of the military information office, Colonel Svenson and Major Robertsson to revisit Sector North, Sector South, as well as parts of central Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then, yeah, between January and July there were several short visits to Sector North, because it was closely located, as well as, okay, before May 1995 Sector West as well as Sector East. And during the third or the fourth week of August, I visited, together with a Belgian UNMO colleague, the Bihac area again, as well as former Sector North and former Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Part of that last trip, did you also go to Knin?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. If I remember well, we went twice to Knin. First on our trip down because we ended up in Split. Split was our last halt and then we returned. So, during the first part of the trip we drove through Knin and we visited the UNMO headquarters there. And during the second trip, so the trip back from Split to Zagreb, we drove through Knin without further in -- yeah, further stops in any headquarters. Also, I'm sorry if I've been confusing. In January 1995, this trip through Sector North and Sector South also went through Knin. So I saw Knin in January as well as end of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, obviously we're not leading evidence on facts from this witness but I wanted to be transparent with you because, you know, he is an expert and he provided an expert report and I thought it was important for you to know that the witness was actually there, and Defence might well explore that in cross-examination, but I won't at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on -- let's move on to other parts of -- aspects of your expertise. Have you ever written academically on the subject of Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while I was serving in the UNTAES mission in Eastern Croatia between July 1996 and May 1997, I was invited by a person I remember -- I knew from the UNPROFOR times who worked for the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik in Germany, to draft an article or -- on military aspects of the UNTAES mission; and that article was then subsequently published in a small booklet which included also contributions from other people, mainly civilian, on developments in the former Yugoslavia. I think it was published sometime -- I believe in -- in the early half of 1997, but I believe also that the Defence has received a copy of that article during our informal meeting in January of this year. And it's obvious when I was working in Belgium, you don't -- when you're working as a military intelligence analyst, you don't publish articles because it is difficult to draw a distinction between what you learn through professional activities and what you may have learned through your private activities, while meeting people working on the same area but in a different environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you invited to conferences, and if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean during that time-period or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Both aspects.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, the conferences at that -- prior to my arrival at ICTY are subject to the same restrictions I explained earlier. There were certain conferences but they were held in a closed environment. In September 2008, I spoke at a conference in Oslo about the use of military expertise in investigation and -- in investigation of serious violations of the laws of war and I drafted a -- I compiled an article for that conference, but it is still at a draft stage and it has not been published yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let's go to the methodology you employed when drafting the report which is the subject of -- of your testimony. Can you give us a brief overview of the material that you consulted in preparing the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the material I consulted to prepare the report is also addressed in the section scope of the report and covers the following categories of document. First of all, military documents. They include what I would describe as doctrine documents, i.e., legislation, regulations, military manuals, and so on. The second category are command documents; I mean by that, orders. Third category of military documents are reporting documents, and as the name says, these are situation reports, war diaries, operational diaries and similar reports. These are mainly reports that -- documents, I apologise, that were prepared by the Croatian armed forces. I mean by that the Main Staff of the Croatian armed forces, the Split Military District, as well as the subordinate units of the Split Military District. I also consulted documents -- I mean military documents from the same categories in relation to the Knin garrison, as well as the special police, while limited myself, for what the month of August is concerned, to documents discussing August 1995 -- I apologise, documents discussing the operations and activities of the special police inside and adjacent to the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District. I also consulted open sources. For example, UN reports. I only used reports, UN reports, the so-called reports by the Secretary-General to the Security Council on the implementation of certain UN Security Council resolutions that address particular aspects of the UNPROFOR, UNCRO, UNPF mandate. I also looked at translations we have of Croatian open sources, I mean by that media, but with the exception of one article, I didn't include media reports in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you have access to these documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: When I received -- sorry. When I received the initial tasking, the ten points, I also received Excel spreadsheets which had been prepared by my colleagues military analysts Dai Morris and Andrei Shakhmetov. These spreadsheets included information on the title of the document, the date, the ERN. These spreadsheets were organised by general topic; for example, Split Military District and Storm. A topic could be military police and so on. I used the spreadsheets to familiarise myself with the nature and the volume of the material that was available to the OTP. I also used the spreadsheets to assist me in conducting the searches I subsequently did in the databases or the database systems that are available to the OTP. So what I try to say is that the documents I have included in the report are certainly not just a reflection of the spreadsheets; on the contrary, the spreadsheets provided guidance and that is all. I reviewed many more documents, both in the spreadsheets as well as the databases, as that I could include in the report because I wanted to the keep the report manageable. But I think when I will address the methodology in detail, I will be able to explain how come that certain documents are included in the report and others not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate of how many documents or perhaps even pages you looked at in the process of compiling, drafting these report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I didn't keep statistics, Your Honours, but when I compare the two parts of the report, I think that approximately half to two thirds of the documents I reviewed are included in the report. And I don't know whether there's time but maybe I can explain it when I describe the search criteria I used. I tried to be as broad as possible with the search criteria. I did, for example, a search on Ante Gotovina. It is obvious that many documents will appear which are not necessarily relevant for the report. I did searches on the names of units, on events, locations, dates, numbers of documents. We know that military documents, they always have register number, they often refer to other military documents whereby the number is specified. Well, I used the numbers to do searches. I also used parts of the numbers to look to try to distinguish or identify series of documents. And obviously you come across many search hits whereby not all of them are relevant, but I wanted to be as thorough as possible to avoid that I missed something, because in the other cases I worked for, I was involved in the -- in the investigation so I was already familiar with the material before drafting the report. Here, I was never involved in any investigative activity, so with the exception of the spreadsheets, I had no knowledge of the material that was available to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you conduct searches on the Internet?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. For example, the American military regulations which are accessible through the Internet. There's also some NATO regulations that are accessible. In relation to Croatian armed forces, I remember from working on the Croatian armed forces before that people are proud of the unit that they served and are proud of the activities that that unit conducted, and for example, there are commemorative web sites where one can find information on the activities of that unit. Again, I didn't use that material as such in the report but that was -- I apologise. That provided useful leads to me to guide my other searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you rely on witness statements?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did not rely on witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The main reason, Your Honours, is that from my experience in the ICTY, there may be differences between what the witness says in his or her statement and what the witness then testifies. In addition, I didn't know who the General Gotovina team -- I mean, the Prosecution team would call or not. So even if I could come across a statement where I believed, well, that's useful, if that person doesn't come here to testify, well, I don't think -- at least in my methodology, I think that the value of such a statement would be limited. And if that person would come to testify, well, probably after the filing of report, then there would be the technical problem, well, what if that person changes his or her testimony. I would have to change that entry in my report. My understanding -- no, my conclusions from the material I looked at is that the material is so comprehensive for the aspects or in relation to the aspects that I wanted to address, that there was no requirement, I didn't feel a requirement to include witness statements or other statements of --or public statements even made in open sources of people who may testify or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you include into the two parts of your report and the addendum detailed annotations or cites to the materials that you were relying upon?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, for -- I tried for each and every factual entry to identify at least one source. And by source, I mean a military document. And I hope that that is visible through the footnotes in the report. If possible when I believed that it was really important for the reader to see the original document, I included the literal quotation of that document, in smaller character size, in the report because I felt that was, yeah, very important in order to understand what I was trying to say, i.e., the conclusions I draw and which can be found in the executive summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were any limits put on your access to material by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There were no limits imposed by the Office of the Prosecutor to my access to material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I ask ... Were there any limits imposed by anyone of any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I wouldn't call it limits as such but, for example, there were regulations I would have liked to have access to. I was not able to find, for example, a Croatian armed forces regulation on the implementation of the Laws of Armed Conflict. As I have pointed out in the report, there are other Croatian armed forces regulations that point to important aspects of the international laws of war, but I didn't find a specific regulation. And that was on, for example, on the list I gave to my colleagues who went to visit the archives. I didn't come across a regulation that specified the duties of a Military District Commander. Even though I found regulations dealing with commanders in general, as well as brigade commanders and also Guards Brigade commanders, I would expect that there would also have been a regulation for the Military District Commander. Now as you may have seen in part 1 of the report, for areas where I felt that the material I had available -- material originating from the Croatian armed forces, was maybe not sufficient, I included JNA regulations as well as NATO -- I mean US regulations. I can explain why I did that, but maybe that will draw us too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, the JNA regulations because I -- again, from my previous experience here and also contacts with former JNA officers who one of them -- at least one of them was later subsequently trained in NATO doctrine, I could see a lot of similarity between the different doctrines for the issues I was to deal with. It is also my understanding that many of the officers serving in the HV --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we just have the identity of the JNA officer he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit puzzled, Mr. Kehoe. You say identity of JNA officer where I see on the transcript that the witness talked about JNA officers. Oh, who -- one of them at least, yes. Yes, could you give us the name of that specific JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That officer is Major-General Milovan Zorc who testified in the Strugar case as a military expert. He is of Slovenian nationality. He left the JNA, if I remember well, in 1991, and then with the developments in Slovenia, familiarized himself through official training courses with NATO doctrine. I visited him, for example, also during the compilation of my report for the Milosevic case, or Slobodan Milosevic case. And just to finish the answer to the previous question, it is also my understanding that many of the officers and senior officers serving in the HV had a JNA background and were therefore familiar with JNA doctrine in -- covering the issues I dealt with in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at the clock. We've got two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why did you include US regulations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I included them for the reason I addressed during the first session, i.e., that, at the latest, in 1994, particular relations developed between the Croatian Ministry of Defence and the US authorities, which were visible, for example, through the activities of the MPRI company. Yeah, I want to say in Croatia but the cooperation between MPRI and the HV, as well as the similarity or the coherence between what was mentioned in JNA regulations or doctrine and NATO doctrine. And, as I explained, to cover aspects where I felt that what I had -- the material I had for the HV was incomplete, I therefore used these US regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it's 7.00. We'll finish for the day. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony either already given, or still to be given, and in view of your special position, I would even invite you to -- to keep your conversations with colleagues or members of the Prosecution team to a minimum because it might raise all kind of questions, and although I'm confident, and this Chamber is confident, that you would strictly adhere to the instructions I just gave you, it would certainly be an advantage if we would also avoid whatever discussions about what you discussed with colleagues, whether that would have been touched upon the testimony, yes or no, it's not only a matter of not talking to them but also to avoid any impression that you would have discussed with anyone the content of your testimony. We adjourn, and resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 20th of November, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.
